recent_posts.title: Why I Love Agent Pi
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares why Pi, a minimal coding agent built on four primitives (read, write, edit, bash), resonates with them over more opinionated alternatives like Claude Code. The post argues that small, composable primitives with visible behavior and honest extension points make for more durable, adaptable tooling. The author draws parallels to Unix and Emacs philosophy, explains how Pi integrates naturally with Nix and Emacs workflows, and describes building their own minimal Rust coding agent (OneLoop) to internalize the same design principles. Key insight: the hard parts of a minimal agent are infrastructure problems (context truncation, output formatting, session persistence), not agent design problems.

recent_posts.title: Why simplicity and single sources of truth matter more in the LLM era
recent_posts.summary: Argues that 'oneness' — one source of truth, one obvious path, one clear owner per layer — is a critical design principle that becomes even more important in the LLM era. As code generation lowers the cost of producing code without lowering the cost of ambiguity, systems with scattered validation, multiple workflows, and unclear ownership become dangerous amplifiers of confusion when AI agents operate inside them. The post advocates for reducing the human review surface to invariants, contracts, and executable examples rather than reading all generated code, and for using LLMs to collapse complexity rather than compound it.

recent_posts.title: Emacs as a programmable workbench
recent_posts.summary: A reflection on why Emacs remains valuable as a programmable workbench in an era of LLMs and AI coding agents. The core argument is that Emacs's buffer abstraction unifies disparate work surfaces — terminals, REPLs, diffs, compilation output, notes, and agent interactions — into a single inspectable, programmable environment. Unlike editors with plugin support, Emacs offers unified manipulation through a consistent model (editing, navigation, search, history) and Emacs Lisp throughout, making every behavior readable and extensible. As AI-generated code becomes abundant, the author argues that engineering judgment and the ability to inspect, verify, compose, and promote rough work into reliable artifacts becomes more critical — and Emacs's durable abstractions serve that need well regardless of which new tools emerge.

recent_posts.title: csvx a minimal CSV parser for Clojure and ClojureScript
recent_posts.summary: A lightweight CSV parsing library called csvx, written in under 200 lines of Clojure, supports both Clojure and ClojureScript (Node.js and browser). It offers full control over tokenization, transformation, delimiter characters, file encoding, line count limits, and error handling, with no external dependencies.

recent_posts.title: Hacker news AI coding experience analysis
recent_posts.summary: An analysis of Hacker News discussions on AI coding tools, combining personal experience with data from CamelAI. Key findings: Claude dominates for serious coding work, Cursor faces trust issues from policy changes, and productivity gains are mixed. Experienced developers using AI to amplify existing skills see the most benefit, while beginners over-relying on AI and enterprise users face the most challenges. The post also covers cognitive dependency risks, the rise of open-source alternatives like Void and Tabby, and a practical Emacs + Claude Code terminal setup using the eat package.

recent_posts.title: MCP explained with code
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on walkthrough of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) using TypeScript code. Covers why MCP exists (reducing M*N LLM integration complexity to M+N), how a standalone MCP client and server communicate via JSON-RPC, and how an LLM (Claude) uses MCP tool capabilities to answer user queries. Includes a full ASCII flow diagram and real code snippets for server tool registration, client tool invocation, and LLM message processing with tool use.

recent_posts.title: Getting started with Nix flakes for reproducible dev environments and Docker builds
recent_posts.summary: A practical introduction to Nix as a build and package management system, covering installation with version pinning, using Nix Flakes for reproducible development environments, and building minimal Docker images for CI/CD. The post clarifies Nix terminology (Nix CLI, Nix DSL, Flakes, NixOS), recommends enabling flakes over legacy channels, and provides concrete flake.nix examples for pinning dependencies and generating Docker images deterministically.

recent_posts.title: Google Bard and Emacs
recent_posts.summary: A short walkthrough on integrating Google Bard into Emacs using the `bard-rs` command-line tool. Since Bard lacks an HTTP API, the author uses the `bard-rs` Rust CLI project and writes a small Elisp function (`kprompt-bard`) that wraps it inside Emacs' compilation buffer, allowing users to send prompts (including selected regions) to Bard directly from within Emacs.

recent_posts.title: Atomic commits made easy
recent_posts.summary: A practical workflow for making atomic commits easier. The approach separates changes by their effects: immutable changes (refactors that don't alter behavior) go in one commit, while mutable changes are grouped by logical context so each commit stands alone. The post recommends the commit-patch tool and shows how to integrate it with Emacs, allowing you to selectively stage, split, or edit diff hunks before committing with C-c C-c, and amend commits with C-c C-C.

recent_posts.title: Notes on StrangeLoop 2022
recent_posts.summary: Personal notes from StrangeLoop 2022 conference covering highlights across three categories: developer experience (observability tooling using eBPF, workflow abstractions for distributed systems), programming languages (type-driven code generation, removing monads from Scala business logic), and data-centric problem solving (data-driven human rights investigations). Also notes that 2023 will be the final StrangeLoop conference.
